# dampack <a href="https://darth-git.github.io/dampack/"><img src="man/figures/logo.png" align="right" height="139" alt="dampack website" /></a>

<!-- badges: start -->
[![CRAN status](https://www.r-pkg.org/badges/version/dampack)](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=dampack)
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/DARTH-git/dampack/actions/workflows/check-standard.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/DARTH-git/dampack/actions/workflows/check-standard.yaml)
[![Codecov test coverage](https://codecov.io/gh/DARTH-git/dampack/branch/main/graph/badge.svg)](https://app.codecov.io/gh/DARTH-git/dampack?branch=main)
<!-- badges: end -->

The Decision Analytic Modeling Package (dampack) is a suite of functions for analyzing and visualizing the health economic outputs of mathematical models.

## Why dampack

Decision-analytic models, such as decision trees, Markov cohort models, microsimulations and discrete-event simulations, estimate the costs and health outcomes of a set of strategies. Turning those outputs into the results that cost-effectiveness studies and health technology assessments report takes the same analyses every time: finding the efficient frontier, computing incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs), summarizing the probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA), and estimating the value of collecting more information.

dampack does these analyses in R for any model. It only needs the model's outputs, so it works the same whether the model was written in R or elsewhere. It is developed by the [DARTH workgroup](https://www.darthworkgroup.com/), alongside the DARTH coding framework for decision models ([Alarid-Escudero et al., 2019](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40273-019-00837-x)), for health decision scientists, health economists, and students.

## What it does

- **Cost-effectiveness analysis.** `calculate_icers()` identifies dominated and extendedly dominated strategies and computes ICERs along the efficient frontier; `plot()` draws the frontier.
- **Probabilistic sensitivity analysis.** `make_psa_obj()` stores the PSA output of any model. Its `plot()` and `summary()` methods show the cost-effectiveness plane, `ceac()` computes cost-effectiveness acceptability curves (CEACs) together with the acceptability frontier (CEAF), and `calc_exp_loss()` computes expected loss curves (ELCs), which show in one figure the expected foregone benefit of each strategy, the optimal strategy, and the expected value of perfect information ([Alarid-Escudero et al., 2019](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jval.2019.02.008)).
- **Value of information.** `calc_evpi()` computes the expected value of perfect information (EVPI). `calc_evppi()` estimates the expected value of partial perfect information (EVPPI) with regression metamodels of the PSA ([Strong et al., 2014](https://doi.org/10.1177/0272989X13505910); [Jalal and Alarid-Escudero, 2018](https://doi.org/10.1177/0272989X17715627)), and `calc_evsi()` estimates the expected value of sample information (EVSI) of a future study with the Gaussian approximation approach ([Jalal and Alarid-Escudero, 2018](https://doi.org/10.1177/0272989X17715627)). Both work from the PSA sample you already have, so no further model runs are needed.
- **Deterministic sensitivity analysis.** One-way and two-way analyses come either from the PSA, through metamodels (`owsa()`, `twsa()`), or from running your model directly (`run_owsa_det()`, `run_twsa_det()`), with tornado diagrams and optimal-strategy plots.
- **PSA inputs.** `gen_psa_samp()` draws parameter samples from common distributions, helpers such as `beta_params()` and `gamma_params()` convert means and standard deviations into distribution parameters, and `run_psa()` runs your model over the samples.

## Installation

Install the released version from CRAN:

``` r
install.packages("dampack")
```

Or the development version from GitHub:

``` r
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("DARTH-git/dampack")
```

Installing from GitHub on macOS with a non-US locale may fail with `Error: (converted from warning) Setting LC_CTYPE failed, using "C"`. Running `defaults write org.R-project.R force.LANG en_US.UTF-8` in the terminal fixes it.

## Example

`cancer_psa_data` holds the PSA output of an illustrative model that compares three cancer treatments over 10,000 samples.

```{r example, message = FALSE}
library(dampack)
data("cancer_psa_data")
l_psa <- make_psa_obj(cost = cancer_psa_data$cost,
                      effectiveness = cancer_psa_data$effectiveness,
                      parameters = cancer_psa_data$parameters,
                      strategies = cancer_psa_data$strategies)

# ICERs from the mean costs and QALYs of each strategy
calculate_icers_psa(l_psa)
```

How likely is each strategy to be cost-effective across willingness-to-pay thresholds? The acceptability frontier (squares) marks the strategy with the highest expected net benefit at each threshold.

```{r ceac, fig.alt = "Cost-effectiveness acceptability curves for chemotherapy, radiation and surgery, with the acceptability frontier."}
v_wtp <- seq(0, 200000, by = 10000)
df_ceac <- ceac(l_psa, wtp = v_wtp)
plot(df_ceac)
```

```{r ceac-50k, include = FALSE}
df_ceac_50k <- df_ceac[df_ceac$WTP == 50000, ]
most_likely <- df_ceac_50k$Strategy[which.max(df_ceac_50k$Proportion)]
optimal <- df_ceac_50k$Strategy[df_ceac_50k$On_Frontier]
pr_most_likely <- max(df_ceac_50k$Proportion)
pr_optimal <- df_ceac_50k$Proportion[df_ceac_50k$On_Frontier]
```

The strategy most likely to be cost-effective is not always the optimal one. At a willingness to pay of $50,000 per QALY, `r most_likely` has the highest probability of being cost-effective (`r round(pr_most_likely, 3)`), but `r optimal` has the highest expected net benefit (probability `r round(pr_optimal, 3)`), so `r optimal` is the strategy on the frontier. This is why a CEAC should always be shown with its frontier.

### Expected loss curves

Expected loss curves go one step further. For each strategy, they show the benefit expected to be lost by choosing it instead of the strategy that would turn out best, so they combine how likely a strategy is to be the wrong choice with how much is lost when it is. In a single figure, the strategy with the lowest expected loss is the optimal one, the curves show where the optimal strategy switches across thresholds, and the expected loss of the optimal strategy equals the expected value of perfect information (EVPI). Alarid-Escudero et al. ([2019](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jval.2019.02.008)) describe these advantages of ELCs over CEACs and the CEAF, and recommend reporting them alongside CEACs, the CEAF and the EVPI.

```{r elc, fig.alt = "Expected loss curves for chemotherapy, radiation and surgery on a log scale, with the frontier, which equals the expected value of perfect information."}
df_elc <- calc_exp_loss(l_psa, wtp = v_wtp)
plot(df_elc, n_x_ticks = 10)
```

```{r elc-50k, include = FALSE}
df_elc_50k <- df_elc[df_elc$WTP == 50000, ]
loss_optimal <- df_elc_50k$Expected_Loss[df_elc_50k$On_Frontier]
evpi_50k <- calc_evpi(l_psa, wtp = 50000)$EVPI
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(loss_optimal, evpi_50k)))
```

At $50,000 per QALY, `r optimal` has the lowest expected loss, $`r format(round(loss_optimal), big.mark = ",")` per patient, which is also the EVPI at that threshold.

### Value of research: EVPPI and EVSI from one PSA

The EVPI is the most a decision maker should pay to remove all uncertainty. To decide which research is worth doing, it helps to know how much of that value comes from a few parameters, the EVPPI, and how much a study of a given size would capture, the EVSI. Both usually need nested simulations: running the model again for every possible study result.

dampack avoids them. `calc_evppi()` fits a regression metamodel of the net benefit on the parameters of interest across the PSA samples. `calc_evsi()` uses the Gaussian approximation approach of Jalal and Alarid-Escudero ([2018](https://doi.org/10.1177/0272989X17715627)). A regression metamodel relates the net benefit to the parameters, and a Gaussian approximation of the preposterior distribution tells how much a study of `n` patients would narrow the uncertainty around them. It needs only the PSA sample, and it works for correlated parameters, non-Gaussian distributions, and several parameters informed by one study.

Here the parameters of interest are the probabilities of treatment failure with chemotherapy and with surgery, each estimated from an earlier study of `n0 = 50` patients:

```{r voi}
v_params <- c("pFailChemo", "pFailSurg")
calc_evpi(l_psa, wtp = 100000)
l_evppi <- calc_evppi(l_psa, wtp = 100000, params = v_params,
                      outcome = "nmb", k = 3, progress = FALSE)
l_evppi$df_evppi
l_evsi <- calc_evsi(l_psa, wtp = 100000, params = v_params,
                    outcome = "nmb", k = 3, n0 = 50,
                    n = c(10, 50, 100, 500, 1000), progress = FALSE)
l_evsi$df_evsi
```

```{r voi-check, include = FALSE}
evpi <- calc_evpi(l_psa, wtp = 100000)$EVPI
evppi <- l_evppi$df_evppi$EVPPI
v_evsi <- l_evsi$df_evsi$EVSI
stopifnot(all(diff(v_evsi) > 0), max(v_evsi) < evppi, evppi < evpi)
fmt <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",")
```

At $100,000 per QALY, removing all uncertainty is worth $`r fmt(evpi)` per patient, and `r round(100 * evppi / evpi)`% of that comes from the two failure probabilities. A new study of 10 patients would capture $`r fmt(v_evsi[1])` per patient, and one of 1,000 patients would capture $`r fmt(max(v_evsi))`, close to the EVPPI. Scaled to the population affected by the decision and compared with the cost of each study design, these values show whether a study is worth running, and how large it should be.

## Learn more

The [package website](https://darth-git.github.io/dampack/) has the full [function reference](https://darth-git.github.io/dampack/reference/) and these articles, best read in this order:

1. [Basic Cost Effectiveness Analysis](https://darth-git.github.io/dampack/articles/basic_cea.html)
2. [Probabilistic Sensitivity Analysis](https://darth-git.github.io/dampack/articles/psa_analysis.html)
3. [Value of Information Analysis](https://darth-git.github.io/dampack/articles/voi.html)
4. [Probabilistic Sensitivity Analysis: Generation](https://darth-git.github.io/dampack/articles/psa_generation.html)
5. [Deterministic Sensitivity Analysis: Generation](https://darth-git.github.io/dampack/articles/dsa_generation.html)

The same articles are installed with the package: see `vignette(package = "dampack")`. What changed in each release is in the [news](https://darth-git.github.io/dampack/news/).

## Citation

Run `citation("dampack")` for how to cite the package.

The expected loss curves in dampack, and why they complement CEACs and the CEAF, are described in:

> Alarid-Escudero F, Enns EA, Kuntz KM, Michaud TL, Jalal H. "Time Traveling Is Just Too Dangerous" but Some Methods Are Worth Revisiting: The Advantages of Expected Loss Curves Over Cost-Effectiveness Acceptability Curves and Frontier. *Value in Health*. 2019;22(5):611-618. [doi:10.1016/j.jval.2019.02.008](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jval.2019.02.008)

The Gaussian approximation approach that `calc_evsi()` uses to compute the EVSI from a single PSA sample is described in:

> Jalal H, Alarid-Escudero F. A Gaussian Approximation Approach for Value of Information Analysis. *Medical Decision Making*. 2018;38(2):174-188. [doi:10.1177/0272989X17715627](https://doi.org/10.1177/0272989X17715627)
